Neutral Citation Number: [2026] EWHC 9001 (Comm)

IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE
BUSINESS AND PROPERTY COURTS OF ENGLAND AND WALES
COMMERCIAL COURT (KBD)

Case No: CL-2025-000914

Date: 12 February 2026

Before: MR JUSTICE FICTIONAL

Between:

ALPHA HOLDINGS LIMITED
Claimant

- and -

BETA SERVICES LIMITED
Defendant

JUDGMENT

Introduction

1. This is a claim for sums said to be due under a framework supply agreement
dated 3 March 2023 ("the Framework Agreement"), together with contractual
interest and damages for repudiatory breach. The claimant, Alpha Holdings
Limited ("Alpha"), is a trading company incorporated in England. The defendant,
Beta Services Limited ("Beta"), is a logistics operator incorporated in the same
jurisdiction.

2. The issues for decision are, in short: (i) whether the Framework Agreement
was varied orally in the course of a meeting in September 2024; (ii) whether
Beta was entitled to suspend performance in reliance on clause 14.3; and (iii)
whether Alpha's acceptance of a reduced payment operated as an accord and
satisfaction discharging the balance of the debt.

The factual background

3. The Framework Agreement provided for the supply of warehousing and
distribution services on call-off terms. Each call-off order was to be
confirmed in writing, and clause 4.1 provided that no variation of the
agreement would be effective unless made in writing and signed by an authorised
representative of each party.

4. Between March 2023 and August 2024 the parties performed the Framework
Agreement without material difficulty. Volumes were stable, invoices were
rendered monthly, and payment was generally made within the thirty-day period
stipulated by clause 9.2.

5. In September 2024 the parties met to discuss a reduction in volumes. Alpha's
commercial director gave evidence that at that meeting the parties agreed a
temporary reduction in the minimum volume commitment. Beta's managing director
gave evidence that the discussion was exploratory only and that no agreement was
reached. No note of the meeting was made by either party.

6. From October 2024 Beta rendered invoices calculated on the reduced volume
basis. Alpha paid those invoices without protest for four months. In February
2025 Alpha's newly appointed finance director reviewed the account and asserted
that the full contractual minimum remained payable for the whole of that period.

The issue of oral variation

7. Clause 4.1 is an anti-oral variation clause in familiar terms. The law is
settled that effect is to be given to such a clause according to its terms: a
party who wishes to vary a contract containing such a clause must do so in the
manner the clause prescribes. The commercial purpose of the clause is to avoid
disputes of precisely the kind that have arisen here, in which two witnesses
give honest but irreconcilable accounts of an undocumented conversation.

8. Alpha submits that the conduct of the parties after September 2024 gives rise
to an estoppel precluding Beta from relying on clause 4.1. For an estoppel of
that kind there must be some words or conduct amounting to a clear and
unequivocal representation that the varied terms would be valid notwithstanding
their informality. The mere fact of performance on the varied basis will not
ordinarily suffice, because performance is equally consistent with a temporary
indulgence.

9. On the evidence I am not satisfied that any such representation was made. The
invoices rendered by Beta were consistent with a concession made without
prejudice to its contractual entitlement, and the correspondence contains no
acknowledgement that the Framework Agreement itself had been altered. The claim
to an oral variation therefore fails.

The suspension issue

10. Clause 14.3 entitled Beta to suspend performance if any undisputed sum
remained unpaid for more than sixty days. Beta suspended performance on 4 April
2025. By that date the only sums outstanding were those which Alpha had disputed
in writing in February 2025. A sum that has been disputed in writing is not an
undisputed sum within the meaning of the clause, whatever the merits of the
dispute may later prove to be.

11. It follows that the suspension was not authorised by clause 14.3 and
constituted a breach of the Framework Agreement. Whether that breach was
repudiatory depends on whether it deprived Alpha of substantially the whole
benefit of the contract. The suspension lasted eleven days and was lifted on
notice. Alpha obtained alternative warehousing at a modest additional cost.

12. In those circumstances the breach was serious but not repudiatory. Alpha is
entitled to damages measured by the additional cost of the alternative
warehousing, which the parties have agreed at the sum pleaded in the schedule to
the particulars of claim.

Accord and satisfaction

13. Beta contends that Alpha's acceptance in March 2025 of a payment expressed
to be "in full and final settlement" discharged the balance of the debt. The
doctrine of accord and satisfaction requires an agreement supported by
consideration. Payment of a lesser sum than that which is due is not, without
more, consideration for the discharge of the greater.

14. There is no suggestion here of any additional benefit conferred on Alpha, of
payment by a third party, or of a binding compromise of a genuine dispute as to
the whole of the sum claimed. The defence of accord and satisfaction therefore
fails.

Conclusion

15. There will be judgment for the claimant for the sums outstanding under the
Framework Agreement, together with contractual interest under clause 9.4 and
damages in the agreed sum in respect of the unlawful suspension. I will hear
counsel on the form of order and on costs if these cannot be agreed.
